clue.text: Church based initially on a rock-forming mineral

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word just before it

parts.note: silica (quartz) is a chief constituent of many rocks

explanation.surface: A geology note: some church built on a mineral that makes up rock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Church' looks like it starts the wordplay with CH, but it is the whole definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A basilica is a large oblong church, especially one given special privileges by the Pope.

clue.text: German book by a northern writer

parts.note: N is the abbreviation for northern

explanation.surface: A German volume penned by someone from the north.
explanation.definitionFit: John Buchan was a Scottish writer, author of The Thirty-Nine Steps.

clue.text: A novelist from eastern England

indicators.note: from says the letters are taken out of the words that follow, lying across them

parts.note: the letters run across the two words, from inside the first into the start of the second

explanation.surface: An author who comes from East Anglia.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to think of a novelist born in the east of England; the novelist is simply sitting inside the words.
explanation.definitionFit: Laurence Sterne was the eighteenth-century novelist who wrote Tristram Shandy.

clue.text: In Marseilles a gendarme is a writer

indicators.note: in says the wanted letters lie inside the words that follow, running across them

parts.note: the letters run from the end of the city name, through a, into the start of gendarme

explanation.surface: A French policeman in Marseilles who turns out to be an author.
explanation.walkthrough: The French setting is no accident: the writer hidden here is French, and his name is French words too (le sage, the wise man).
explanation.definitionFit: Alain-René Le Sage was an eighteenth-century French novelist, author of Gil Blas.

clue.text: Poet giving talk on rotten novel

indicators.note: novel means new, so the word before it is given a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A poet delivering a lecture about a dreadful novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rotten novel' reads as a bad book; rotten supplies the letters and novel says to rearrange them.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Chatterton was an eighteenth-century English poet who died at seventeen.

clue.text: Personnel on a Scottish isle

parts.note: the people employed by an organisation

explanation.surface: Workers stationed on a remote island off Scotland.
explanation.walkthrough: Staffa is the small Hebridean island famous for Fingal's Cave.
explanation.definitionFit: Staffa is an uninhabited island in the Inner Hebrides, off the west coast of Scotland.

clue.text: Wild ranter, he may be a writer

indicators.note: something wild is out of control, so the following letters run riot into a new order

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A raving loudmouth who, oddly, might turn out to be an author.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century English poet and religious prose writer.

clue.text: A novelist, perhaps, for trees?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: C.S. ..., who wrote the Hornblower books
second meaning: one who tends woodland, someone who works for trees

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second half: a person whose job is looking after trees.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is both the surname of the author C.S. Forester and the title of a woodland officer.

clue.text: He wrote in Danish and Irish to a Pole

parts.note: Erse is the Gaelic language of Ireland

explanation.surface: A multilingual author writing in Danish and Irish to a Polish correspondent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pole' looks like a Polish person; it is a magnetic pole.
explanation.definitionFit: Hans Christian Andersen, the fairy-tale author, wrote in his native Danish.

clue.text: Piece on board revolutionary vessel going to isle

parts.note: SS, steamship, the prefix to a vessel's name

explanation.surface: Someone on board a rebel ship sailing for an island.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Piece on board' reads as a person aboard ship; the board is a chessboard.
explanation.definitionFit: A chessman is any of the pieces moved on a chessboard.

clue.text: Wild free city

parts.note: wild in the sense of crazy or furious
to free of something is to rid it

explanation.surface: A lawless, untamed town where anything goes.
explanation.definitionFit: Madrid is the capital of Spain, so it is an example of a city.

clue.text: Renounce agent; be a producer

indicators.note: a producer makes something new out of raw material, so the preceding letters are worked into a fresh word

explanation.surface: Advice to someone in show business: drop your agent and start producing.
explanation.walkthrough: The semicolon makes it read as two instructions, but 'agent; be a' is one string of letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To abnegate is to give up or deny oneself something, a formal synonym of renounce.

clue.text: Not so much gold for landlord, perhaps

explanation.surface: A tenant grumbling that the rent money paid to the landlord is less.
explanation.definitionFit: A lessor grants a lease; a landlord letting property is one example, hence the 'perhaps'.

clue.text: A novelist's means of raising capital

explanation.surface: How an author goes about financing a project.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raising capital' reads as fundraising; it splits into a lifting device and a capital city. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Jack London was the American novelist who wrote The Call of the Wild.

clue.text: A relative in the country ain't sophisticated

indicators.note: in places one set of letters inside the country named next

parts.note: a country, the one this clue has in mind

indicators.note: sophisticated can mean altered or adulterated, so the letters it follows are tampered with

parts.note: the letters of the contraction, apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A country cousin who never picked up city polish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ain't sophisticated' reads as a judgement of the relative; in fact 'sophisticated' scrambles the letters of ain't.
explanation.definitionFit: A great-niece is the granddaughter of one's brother or sister, a family relation.

clue.text: Howard's End and The Ascent of Man are produced by a writer

indicators.note: the end of Howard's is its closing letter
in a down clue an ascent reads upwards, so the word for man is turned round

explanation.surface: Two famous books, Forster's novel and Bronowski's TV history, credited to one author.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals dress the words up as book titles. The 'The' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Walter de la Mare was an English poet and story writer, author of The Listeners.

clue.text: Novelist or cave-dweller with hope but no aspiration

indicators.note: aspiration is the breathy h sound, so losing it drops that letter

parts.note: trolls live in caves in folklore

explanation.surface: A writer, or a hopeful but unambitious troglodyte.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No aspiration' reads as lacking ambition; it means dropping the h sound.
explanation.definitionFit: Anthony Trollope was the Victorian novelist of the Barsetshire series.

clue.text: Irish writer producing Danish novel about the queen

indicators.note: about means going around, so the rearranged letters surround the queen
novel means new, so the word before it takes a new arrangement

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An Irish author writing a Danish novel about a queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Danish novel' reads as a book from Denmark; novel is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Brinsley Sheridan, born in Dublin, wrote The Rivals and The School for Scandal.

clue.text: Fortifications for electrical component factory

parts.note: the earth wire or connection in a circuit
a works is an industrial plant

explanation.surface: A defence plant making parts for electrical goods.
explanation.walkthrough: Earth is the British term for an electrical ground connection.
explanation.definitionFit: Earthworks are banks and ditches of soil built as military defences.

clue.text: Plagiarise sound writer?

indicators.note: sound tells us the word is identified by how it is spoken

parts.note: to plagiarise is to steal someone's words

explanation.surface: Is copying someone else's work a sound move for an author?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sound writer' looks like a reliable author; sound is the homophone signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Steele was the Irish-born essayist who co-founded The Spectator.

clue.text: Some degree necessary for a writer

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so a part of the following words is taken

parts.note: the letters straddle the two words

explanation.surface: An author needs some sort of university qualification.
explanation.definitionFit: Graham Greene was the English novelist of Brighton Rock and The Power and the Glory.

clue.text: German and Swedish leader and French and Norwegian novelist

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its opening letter

explanation.surface: A pan-European line-up of German, Swedish, French and Norwegian figures.
explanation.walkthrough: 'German and' looks like a list beginning; it is the German word for and.
explanation.definitionFit: Sigrid Undset was the Norwegian novelist who won the 1928 Nobel Prize in Literature.

clue.text: The fascination of everything on a river

parts.note: the Ure, a river in Yorkshire, joins on after

explanation.surface: Musing on why everything about river life is so appealing.
explanation.walkthrough: The Ure is a Yorkshire river, a crossword favourite.
explanation.definitionFit: Allure is the quality of being powerfully attractive, the same idea as fascination.

clue.text: Wine going to Ireland or beer in Manx resort

parts.note: Erin is the poetic name for Ireland
an alternative route to the same letters, porter (a dark beer) plus in, so nothing new is added

explanation.surface: Choosing between wine and Irish beer while on holiday on the Isle of Man.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue offers a second route, 'or beer in': PORTER (a dark beer) plus IN gives the same letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Port Erin is a seaside village and resort in the south-west of the Isle of Man.

clue.text: Escapes, as there's a gap on the middle

indicators.note: something set on the middle sits between the outer parts, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: taken as written, the letters that go round
a void is an empty space

explanation.surface: A getaway explained: there was a hole in the middle to slip through.
explanation.definitionFit: To avoid something is to escape or evade it, so the verbs match in the third person.

clue.text: Lack of work for one with endless shift

indicators.note: to shift is to move things around, so the word before it is rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Somebody stuck on an interminable shift yet with nothing to do.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Endless' looks like a deletion signal for shift, but it is the word whose letters get rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Idleness is the state of being inactive or unemployed, having no work.

clue.text: They leave an English flower on a French treetop

parts.note: a flower is a river (it flows); the Exe runs through Devon in England

indicators.note: the top of a word written down is its opening letter, so only that is kept

explanation.surface: A botanical tableau: an English bloom perched on a French treetop.
explanation.walkthrough: Flower is the crossword river, something that flows. The answer is the Latin stage direction.
explanation.definitionFit: Exeunt is the stage direction meaning that several actors go off stage.

clue.text: Unseemly characters in den, etc.

indicators.note: characters here are letters taken individually, free to be set down in another order

parts.note: taken as written, as letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Disreputable types gathering in a den of vice and so on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Characters' looks like people in the den; it means letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Indecent means improper or offending against decorum, a synonym of unseemly.
